newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil states to privatize $5-10 bln in '97.
newsitem.headline: Brazil states to privatize $5-10 bln in '97.

text.p: Brazilian states will privatize assets worth between $5 billion and $10 billion in 1997, said Finance Ministry Executive Secretary Pedro Parente.

"We could have a number comparable to the $10 billion to be raised in federal privatizations," Parente said. He added that of the total revenue raised by states through privatizations, at least $5 billion would be used toward paying down the nation's mammoth domestic debt stock.

Speaking to foreign correspondents, Parente said he also expected the share of public sector operational deficit held by Brazilian states and municipalities to drop by 40 percent in 1997. The operational balance includes interest payments on government debt.

Figures released earlier Monday showed that Brazil's total operational deficit was 3.98 percent of GDP in the January to October period. The states and municipalities had an operational deficit of 2.18 percent of GDP in the period.

Parente said he was confident states would manage to keep spending down next year because 30 percent to 50 percent of their contributions to this year's total deficit stemmed from public sector pay rises awarded in mid-1995, which were not granted in 1996.

He also said the government was discussing debt renegotiation deals with six states, including Rio de Janeiro, that were similar to accords reached with nine other states and approved last week by the Senate.

The nine states, including major debtors Sao Paulo, Minas Gerais and Rio Grande do Sul, have agreed to privatize assets, increase taxes and take other cost-cutting measures in return for easier repayment schedules.

Parente added that the government would try to end 1997 with a primary budget surplus of about 1.5 percent of GDP. The primary balance, which excludes payments on government debt, encompasses the three levels of government, state owned companies and the social security system. Privatization revenue is not included in the primary balance.

Parente said that Brazilian officials and the International Monetary Fund determined that a 1.5 percent primary surplus would not only stop the nation's rising debt-to-GDP ratio but that it could also cause the ratio to decline.
He said the primary surplus should rise to 2 percent of GDP from 1998 onwards.
